Effect of a structured walking programme on recovery after hip replacement surgery: a randomised controlled trial

Recovery after total hip replacement depends on early mobilisation, patient education and consistent follow-up. We conducted a single-centre randomised trial to test whether a structured walking programme delivered by physiotherapists improved functional outcomes at twelve weeks compared with usual care.

Adults scheduled for elective total hip replacement between March 2019 and November 2021 were screened for eligibility. Patients with an active infection, severe cognitive impairment or a body mass index above forty were excluded. Participants were allocated in a one to one ratio using a computer generated sequence that was concealed from the recruiting staff. The intervention consisted of supervised walking sessions three times a week for six weeks, followed by a home programme that was reinforced by telephone calls every fortnight. The control group received the standard booklet and the usual outpatient appointments. The primary outcome was the six minute walk distance at twelve weeks. Secondary outcomes included the timed up and go test, the Harris hip score and a patient reported measure of pain. Assessors who collected the outcome data were unaware of the group assignment.

A total of 214 patients were randomised. Baseline characteristics were similar between the two groups. Attendance at the supervised sessions was high, and only nine participants withdrew before the twelve week assessment. Participants who missed more than two supervised sessions were still included in the analysis, and a sensitivity analysis that excluded them produced the same conclusion. The primary outcome improved in both groups, but the gain was larger in the intervention group. The six minute walk distance increased by 48 metres in the intervention group and by 21 metres in the control group. The difference remained after adjustment for age, sex and baseline function. Secondary outcomes favoured the intervention, although the effect on pain was small and did not reach the prespecified threshold. Core temperatures in the recovery room were recorded at 30, 60, and 120 minutes after admission, and no participant developed a fever. Adverse events were rare and were equally distributed. No serious adverse events were attributed to the walking programme.

The findings suggest that a structured walking programme can be delivered safely after hip replacement and that it produces a modest improvement in walking capacity. The effect is smaller than the one reported in an earlier trial that compared supervised sessions vs unsupervised home exercises. Several limitations deserve comment. The trial was conducted in a single hospital, the follow-up was limited to twelve weeks, and the physiotherapists could not be blinded. The pre and post operative scores were available for most but not all participants. Future studies should test whether the programme can be maintained at lower cost and whether the benefit persists after one year.
